### Deadlines for your tax return

HMRC must receive your tax return and any money you owe by the deadline. 

If you do not know your profit for the whole tax year, you still need to send a tax return. Check how to send a return if you do not know your profit for the whole year.

The last tax year started on 6 April 2025 and ended on 5 April 2026. The deadline for earlier tax returns has passed and you may have to pay a penalty. Send your tax return or payment as soon as possible to avoid further penalties.

## Telling HMRC you need to complete a return

You must tell HMRC by 5 October if you need to complete a tax return for the last year and:

- you have not sent a tax return before

- you registered before but did not need to send a tax return for the 2024 to 2025 tax year

You can tell HMRC by registering for Self Assessment. Check how to register for Self Assessment.

### If you register after 5 October 2026

HMRC will send you a letter or email with a new deadline for your tax return. This deadline will be 3 months from the date on the letter or email.

You must still pay the tax you owe by 11:59pm on 31 January 2027. If you do not, you will get a penalty.

## Sending a paper tax return

HMRC must receive your paper tax return by 11:59pm on 31 October 2026. If they do not, you will get a late filing penalty. 

You can send your return on or after 6 April 2026, as long as HMRC receives it by the deadline.

## Submitting an online tax return

You must send your online tax return by 11:59pm on 31 January 2027. If you do not, you will get a penalty for late filing.

If you want to pay your Self Assessment bill through your tax code, you must send your return by 11:59pm on 30 December 2026. If you miss this deadline, you will have to pay another way.

You can send your return at any time on or after 6 April 2026 up to the deadline.

## Paying the tax you owe

You must pay your Self Assessment tax by 11:59pm on 31 January 2027. If you do not, you will get a penalty.

There is a second deadline of 31 July if you make ‘payments on account’ towards your bill.

You can estimate your Self Assessment tax bill before you send your tax return to:

- give you an idea of what your bill may be
- help you budget and pay on time

Find help to understand the tax you owe.

## Trustees of a registered pension scheme or non-resident companies

HMRC must receive a paper tax return by 31 January 2027. You cannot send a return online.

You can send your return at any time on or after 6 April 2026, if HMRC receives it by the deadline.

### Partnership returns if you have a company as a partner

If your partnership’s accounting date is between 1 February and 5 April, and one of your partners is a limited company, there are deadlines for your returns.

- The deadline for online returns is 12 months from the accounting date.
- The deadline for paper returns is 9 months from the accounting date.

### Penalties

You will get a penalty if you need to complete a tax return and you:

- send your return late
- pay your tax bill late

You can estimate your penalty for late Self Assessment tax returns and payments.

## If you register for Self Assessment late

If you register after 5 October and you do not pay all of your tax bill by 31 January, you may get a ‘failure to notify’ penalty. 

The penalty is based on the amount you still owe. You will receive the penalty within 12 months after HMRC gets your Self Assessment tax return.

You can find more information about ‘failure to notify’ penalties.

## If you send your tax return late

You will get these penalties for sending your tax return late:

- An initial penalty of £100.
- After 3 months, you will get daily penalties of £10 per day, up to a maximum of £900.
- After 6 months, you will get a further penalty of either 5% of the tax due or £300, whichever is greater.
- After 12 months, you will get another penalty of either 5% of the tax due or £300, whichever is greater.

To avoid this, send your Self Assessment tax return as soon as possible.

All partners will be charged a penalty if a partnership tax return is late.

## If you pay your tax late

You will get 3 penalties. Each penalty is 5% of the tax you have not paid. You get these penalties at:

* 30 days
* 6 months
* 12 months

You will also be charged interest on the money you owe. Pay your Self Assessment tax bill as soon as possible to avoid these charges.

Find out what happens if you do not pay your tax bill.

### Your State Pension amount

The amount you get for your State Pension depends on your National Insurance record. 

Check your State Pension forecast to see what you could get when you reach State Pension age. This forecast also shows your National Insurance record.

The full rate of the new State Pension is £241.30 a week. Your amount may be different if:

- you were contracted out before 2016
- of the number of National Insurance qualifying years you have 
- you paid into the Additional State Pension before 2016

Find out what tax you could pay on your retirement income, including if you retire abroad.

## If you get less than £241.30 a week

You may need more years of National Insurance contributions to increase your State Pension.

### If your National Insurance record started before April 2016

You may have been 'contracted out'. While you were contracted out, you or your employer paid more into your workplace or private pension. You paid less into your State Pension.

If you were contracted out, you will usually need more than 35 qualifying years to get the full rate of the new State Pension.

### If your National Insurance record started after April 2016

If your National Insurance record started after April 2016, you will need 35 qualifying years to get the full rate of the new State Pension.

## If you’re getting more than £241.30 a week

If you paid into the Additional State Pension before 2016 and you would have got more State Pension using the old rules, you will get a ‘protected payment’. This payment is added to your full rate of new State Pension.

## Annual increases

The new State Pension increases each year. It goes up by the highest of these three:

- earnings – the average percentage growth in wages in Great Britain
- prices – the percentage growth in prices in the UK, measured by the Consumer Prices Index (CPI)
- 2.5%

If you have a protected payment, it increases each year in line with the CPI.

### Child Benefit rates

There are 2 Child Benefit rates.

| Who the allowance is for | Rate (weekly) |
| :--- | :--- |
| Eldest or only child | £27.05 |
| Additional children | £17.90 per child |

You must contact the Child Benefit Office if you are paid too much or too little.

Any Child Benefit payments you get will count towards the benefit cap. If you are affected by the cap, you will still get the full amount for your Child Benefit payments, but your other benefits may be reduced.

## If families split up

If a family splits up, you get £27.05 a week for the eldest child.

If you have 2 children and one lives with you and the other lives with someone else, such as an ex-partner, you will each get £27.05 a week.

If both of you claim for the same child, only one of you will get Child Benefit for them.

If you are entitled to Child Benefit for any other children, you will get £17.90 for each child.

## If families join together

If you move in with a partner who also claims Child Benefit, you will get £27.05 for the eldest child in the household. You will get £17.90 for any younger children. 

You and your partner can claim for different children. You cannot both claim at the higher rate if you live together. You may have to pay back some of the money if you do. 

You must report the change to your family circumstances.

## If you or your partner earn over the threshold

If either you or your partner has an ‘adjusted net income’ over the threshold, you may have to pay the High Income Child Benefit Charge.

Your adjusted net income is your total taxable income before personal allowances and minus things like Gift Aid. Your total taxable income includes money from interest on savings and dividends.

If you have to pay the charge, you can still get other benefits of Child Benefit, such as National Insurance credits. The charge will not be more than the total amount of Child Benefit money you get.

Use the Child Benefit tax calculator to see if your adjusted net income is over the threshold. If it is, the calculator will show how much you must pay.

If both you and your partner earn over the threshold, the person with the higher adjusted net income must pay the charge.

If either you or your partner has an income of £20,000 or more above the threshold (£10,000 or more before April 2024), you will be charged the same amount that you get in Child Benefit payments. This means you will get no extra money from Child Benefit.

You can claim Child Benefit but choose not to get the payments if you do not want to pay the charge. You will still get other benefits, such as National Insurance credits.

## If you’re under 16

You can either claim for your own child or someone responsible for you can claim for them on your behalf. You will usually get more money if you claim yourself.

### How much you get

Universal Credit is paid once a month. The amount you get depends on:

* your standard allowance
* any extra amounts that apply to you
* any money taken off your payment
* if you’re working, how much you earn

You can use a benefits calculator to see how much you may get.

If you get Universal Credit, you will earn Class 3 National Insurance credits. These credits count towards your State Pension.

## Standard allowance

Your household will get one standard allowance.

| How much you’ll get | Monthly standard allowance |
| :--- | :--- |
| If you’re single and under 25 | £338.58 |
| If you’re single and 25 or over | £424.90 |
| If you live with your partner and you’re both under 25 | £528.34 (for you both) |
| If you live with your partner and either of you are 25 or over | £666.97 (for you both) |

## Extra amounts

You may get extra money on top of your standard allowance if you are eligible.

You must report changes when you become eligible for extra money. Payments are not added automatically. For example, if you become a carer, you must tell the DWP. The Universal Credit carer’s element is not added automatically if you start getting Carer’s Allowance.

### If you have children

You will get £303.94 a month for each child living with you.

If your first child was born before 6 April 2017, you will get an extra £47.94 a month for that child.

You get money for each child until the 31 August after their:

- 16th birthday

- 19th birthday, if they are in eligible education or training – for example, they are studying for GCSEs, A levels, BTECs, Scottish Highers and SVQs or NVQs up to level 3

### If your child has a disability

You may get an extra monthly amount if any of your children are disabled.

You will either get:

- £164.79 - the lower amount

- £514.71 - the higher amount

The higher amount is for a child who:

- gets the highest rate of the care component of Disability Living Allowance (DLA) for children

- gets the higher rate of the daily living part of Personal Independence Payment (PIP)

- is blind or severely sight impaired

The lower amount is for a child who gets any other rate of either DLA for children, or PIP.

### Childcare costs

You can claim back up to 85% of your childcare costs if you are working. If you live with your partner, both of you need to be working, unless one of you cannot work due to a disability or health condition.

The childcare must be from a registered provider. You can get help paying for childcare including nurseries, childminders, breakfast clubs, after school care and holiday clubs.

The most you can get each month is:

- £1,071.09 for one child

- £1,836.16 for 2 or more children

You must pay your childcare costs up front and claim the money back as part of your payment. You can get support to help you pay your childcare costs up front. Talk to your work coach after you have made your claim.

Read more about childcare costs and Universal Credit.

### If you have a disability or health condition

You may get an extra monthly amount if you cannot work because of a health condition, disability or long-term illness.

| How much you’ll get | Extra monthly amount |
| :--- | :--- |
| If you have a severe health condition or disability that’s unlikely to change or you are nearing the end of your life | £429.80 |
| If your health condition or disability is assessed as less severe or your condition may improve over time | £217.26 |

There are different rules if you reported a health condition before 6 April 2026.

If you live with your partner and you both have limited capability for work and work-related activity, you will only get one extra monthly amount. You will get the higher amount if either of you is eligible for it.

If you get the severe disability premium and you are moving to Universal Credit, you may also be entitled to a ‘transitional protection’ payment.

Read more about health conditions, disability and Universal Credit.

### If you care for someone who gets a health or disability-related benefit

You could get an extra amount called a ‘carer’s element’. This is added to your Universal Credit if you care for someone who gets one of the following benefits:

- Adult Disability Payment – standard or enhanced award

- Armed Forces Independence Payment 

- Attendance Allowance

- Child Disability Payment – middle or highest care award

- Constant Attendance Allowance - full day rate, intermediate rate or exceptional rate with Industrial Injuries Disablement Benefit

- Constant Attendance Allowance - full day rate with a War Disablement Pension

- Disability Living Allowance – middle or highest care rate

- Personal Independence Payment – either rate of the daily living part

You must provide care for them for at least 35 hours a week.

You will get an extra monthly amount of £209.34. If you live with your partner and you both care for the same person, you will only get one extra monthly amount.

You may also be eligible for Carer’s Allowance.

This is on top of any extra amount you get if you have a disabled child.

If you are getting an extra amount because you have limited capability for work and work related activity (LCWRA), you cannot also get the carer’s element.

If the person you care for gets the severe disability premium, it will stop when you claim the carer’s element of Universal Credit.

### Housing costs

You could get money to help pay your housing costs. The payment can cover rent and some service charges.

If you are a homeowner, you might be able to get a loan to help with interest payments on your mortgage.

## Money taken off your payment

We may reduce your payments if any of these apply:

- you are paying back an advance on a Universal Credit payment
- you would get more than the limit set by the benefit cap
- you were paid too much in benefits in the past
- you owe money for Council Tax, court fines, electricity, gas, water or Child Maintenance
- you pay your gas or electricity bill directly from your Universal Credit payment
- you have a paid job
- you have other income, such as money from pensions or certain other benefits
- you have more than £6,000 in money, savings and investments

If you have more than £6,000 in money, savings and investments, your payment will go down by £4.35 for every £250 you have between £6,000 and £16,000. We also take off another £4.35 for any part of your money that is not a full £250.

Find out more about money taken off your Universal Credit payment.

### Benefits that affect how much Universal Credit you get

You can get Universal Credit at the same time as other benefits. We will reduce your Universal Credit payment by the same amount as the other benefit payment you receive. This rule applies if you get Universal Credit and any of these benefits:

- Armed Forces Pensions
- Carer’s Allowance
- Carer Support Payment (Scotland)
- Incapacity Benefit
- Industrial Injuries Disablement Benefit (excluding any increases for constant attendance or exceptionally severe disablement)
- Maternity Allowance
- Severe Disablement Allowance
- State Pension
- Widowed Mother’s Allowance
- Widowed Parent’s Allowance
- New Style Employment and Support Allowance (ESA)
- New Style Jobseeker’s Allowance (JSA)

## Claiming Universal Credit and New Style ESA or JSA

You may be able to get Universal Credit at the same time as New Style ESA or JSA. If you do, your Universal Credit payment will be reduced by the amount of money you get for New Style ESA or JSA.

New Style ESA and JSA are paid more often than Universal Credit.

You will also get different National Insurance credits. These count towards your State Pension and can help you qualify for other benefits.

You may still get New Style ESA or JSA if your circumstances change and your Universal Credit payment is reduced or stops. For example, this could happen if:

- your partner’s income increases

- you have more than £16,000 in savings

Check if you are eligible for:

- New Style Jobseeker’s Allowance

- New Style Employment and Support Allowance

## Moving to Universal Credit from other benefits

If you have applied for Universal Credit, you will keep getting your current benefit for 2 more weeks. You must still be eligible for your current benefit for this to happen.

This rule only applies if you are getting income-related Employment and Support Allowance or Housing Benefit.

You will not need to pay back these extra payments. These payments will not affect the Universal Credit you might get.

If you have received a Migration Notice letter telling you to claim Universal Credit, you may also get a ‘transitional protection’ payment.

## If your Universal Credit claim is reviewed

We may review your claim. This is to make sure you get the right payment and the right support. You can find out more about Universal Credit reviews.

### Eligibility

You may get Carer’s Allowance if you, the person you care for, and the type of care you provide meet certain rules.

## The person you care for

The person you care for must get one of these benefits:

- Personal Independence Payment - daily living component
- Disability Living Allowance - the middle or highest care rate
- Scottish Adult Disability Living Allowance - the middle or highest care rate
- Attendance Allowance
- Pension Age Disability Payment
- Constant Attendance Allowance at or above the normal maximum rate with an Industrial Injuries Disablement Benefit
- Constant Attendance Allowance at the basic (full day) rate with a War Disablement Pension
- Armed Forces Independence Payment
- Child Disability Payment - the middle or highest care rate
- Adult Disability Payment - daily living component at the standard or enhanced rate

### If you care for the person with others

You cannot get Carer’s Allowance if you share their care and the other carer is already claiming:

- Carer’s Allowance for that person
- Carer Support Payment for that person
- the extra amount of Universal Credit for caring for someone who gets a disability-related benefit for that person

If you want to get Carer’s Allowance, talk to the other carer about changing their benefits.

If the other carer does not want to do that, you can still apply for Carer’s Allowance. The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) will decide who should receive it.

## The type of care you provide

You must spend at least 35 hours a week caring for someone. This can include:

- helping with washing and cooking
- taking the person you care for to a doctor’s appointment
- helping with household tasks, such as managing bills and shopping

## Your eligibility

All of these rules must apply to you:

- you are 16 or over
- you spend at least 35 hours a week caring for someone
- you have been in England, Scotland or Wales for at least 2 of the last 3 years (this rule does not apply if you are a refugee or have humanitarian protection status)
- you normally live in England or Wales, or you live abroad as a member of the armed forces (you might still be eligible if you are moving to or already living in an EEA country or Switzerland)
- you are not in full-time education
- you are not studying for 21 hours a week or more
- you are not subject to immigration control
- your earnings are £204 or less a week after tax, National Insurance and expenses

If you live in Scotland, you must apply for Carer Support Payment instead of Carer’s Allowance.

If you are from the EU, Switzerland, Norway, Iceland or Liechtenstein, you and your family usually also need settled or pre-settled status under the EU Settlement Scheme to get Carer’s Allowance. The deadline to apply was 30 June 2021 for most people, but you might still be able to apply. Check if you can still apply to the EU Settlement Scheme.

### Calculating your earnings

Your earnings are any money from work and self-employment after tax, National Insurance and expenses.

Expenses can include:

- 50% of your pension contributions
- equipment you need to do your job (for example, specialist clothing)
- travel costs between different workplaces that your employer does not pay for (for example, fuel or train fares)
- business costs if you are self-employed (for example, a computer you only use for work)

If you pay a carer to look after the disabled person or your children while you work, you can count care costs that are less than or equal to 50% of your earnings as an expense. The carer cannot be your spouse, partner, parent, child or sibling.

Payments that do not count as earnings include:

- money from an occupational or private pension
- money for your living or accommodation costs from someone you live with (this person cannot be a tenant or boarder)
- the first £20 a week and 50% of the rest of any income you make from someone boarding in your home
- a loan or advance payment from your employer

## If you get State Pension

You cannot get the full amount of both Carer’s Allowance and your State Pension at the same time.

* If your pension is £86.45 a week or more, you will not get a Carer’s Allowance payment.
* If your pension is less than £86.45 a week, you will get a Carer’s Allowance payment to make up the difference.

## If you get Pension Credit

If your State Pension is more than £86.45 a week, you will not get Carer’s Allowance. Instead, your Pension Credit payments will increase.

### Pension Credit

Pension Credit adds to your weekly income:

*   to £238 if you are single
*   to £363.25 if you have a partner

You may get extra amounts if you have other responsibilities and costs.

The top up and extra amounts are known as ‘Guarantee Credit’.

## If you have a severe disability

You may get an extra £86.05 a week if you get any of the following:

- Attendance Allowance 
- the middle or highest rate of the care component of Disability Living Allowance (DLA)
- the daily living component of Personal Independence Payment (PIP)
- Armed Forces Independence Payment
- the daily living component of Adult Disability Payment
- Pension Age Disability Payment
- the middle or highest rate of the care component of Scottish Adult Disability Living Allowance

## If you care for another adult

You may get an extra £48.15 a week if:

* you get Carer’s Allowance
* you get Carer Support Payment
* you have claimed Carer’s Allowance but you are not being paid because you already get another benefit that pays a higher amount

If you and your partner have both claimed or are both getting Carer’s Allowance, you can both get this extra amount.

## If you’re responsible for children or young people

You will get an extra amount for each child or young person living with you.

You will get £69.98 a week for each child or young person. This becomes £81.07 a week for the first child if they were born before 6 April 2017.

You will get this extra amount until the 31 August after their:

- 16th birthday
- 19th birthday, if they are in eligible education or training, such as GCSEs, A levels, BTECs, Scottish Highers, SVQs or NVQs up to level 3

If they are in education, it must be for more than 12 hours a week on average.

### If the child or young person is disabled

If your child or young person is disabled, you could get extra money.

You could get an extra £37.93 a week if they get:

- Disability Living Allowance (DLA) for children: lowest or middle rate of the care component, or any rate of the mobility component
- Child Disability Payment: lowest or middle rate of the care component, or any rate of the mobility component
- Scottish Adult Disability Living Allowance: lowest or middle rate of the care component, or any rate of the mobility component
- Personal Independence Payment (PIP): standard rate of the daily living component, or any rate of the mobility component
- Adult Disability Payment: standard rate of the daily living component, or any rate of the mobility component

You could get an extra £118.46 a week if they get:

- Disability Living Allowance (DLA) for children: highest rate of the care component
- Child Disability Payment: highest rate of the care component
- Scottish Adult Disability Living Allowance: highest rate of the care component
- Personal Independence Payment (PIP): enhanced rate of the daily living component
- Adult Disability Payment: enhanced rate of the daily living component

You might also be eligible if they are blind or severely sight impaired.

## If you have housing costs

You may get extra money to help pay for your housing costs. This can include:

- ground rent if you have a leasehold property
- some service charges
- charges for tents and site rents

The amount you may get depends on what your housing costs are.

If you get Pension Credit, you can also apply for these:

- Council Tax Reduction
- Housing Benefit if you rent the property you live in
- Support for Mortgage Interest if you own the property you live in

## If you have savings or a second pension

You may get the ‘Savings Credit’ part of Pension Credit if both of these apply:

- you reached State Pension age before 6 April 2016
- you saved money for your retirement, like a personal or workplace pension

If you are single, you will get up to £17.96 a week in Savings Credit. If you have a partner, you will get up to £20.10 a week.

You may still get some Savings Credit even if you do not get the Guarantee Credit part of Pension Credit.

## Other help if you get Pension Credit

If you get Pension Credit, you will automatically get Cold Weather Payments.

You can also:

- 
apply for a free TV licence if you are aged 75 or over

- 
get help with NHS costs if you get the Guarantee Credit part of Pension Credit

NHS costs can include things such as prescriptions, dental treatment, glasses and transport costs for hospital appointments.

## Get help with extra amounts

Call the Pension Service helpline if you are not sure if you can get extra amounts.

Pension Service helpline

Telephone: 0800 99 1234

Relay UK: 18001 then 0800 99 1234 (if you cannot hear or speak on the phone)

British Sign Language (BSL) video relay service if you are on a computer - find out how to use the service on mobile or tablet

Monday to Friday, 8am to 6pm (except public holidays)

Find out about call charges

### Statutory Maternity Pay (SMP)

You can get Statutory Maternity Pay (SMP) for up to 39 weeks.

You get:

* 90% of your average weekly earnings (before tax) for the first 6 weeks
* £194.32 or 90% of your average weekly earnings (whichever is lower) for the next 33 weeks

SMP is paid in the same way as your wages, for example monthly or weekly. Tax and National Insurance will be deducted.

Use the maternity planner to work out how much maternity pay you may get.

If you take Shared Parental Leave you will get Statutory Shared Parental Pay (ShPP). ShPP is £194.32 a week or 90% of your average weekly earnings, whichever is lower.

## Start date

SMP usually starts when you take your maternity leave.

It starts automatically if you are off work for a pregnancy-related illness in the 4 weeks before the week (Sunday to Saturday) that your baby is due.

## Problems and disputes

Ask your employer to explain your SMP if you think it is not right. If you disagree about the amount, or if your employer cannot pay (for example because they are insolvent), you should contact the Statutory Payment Disputes Team.

### Statutory Sick Pay (SSP)

If you are eligible, you can get £123.25 a week Statutory Sick Pay (SSP) or 80% of your normal weekly earnings, whichever is lower. It is paid for up to 28 weeks.

You will be paid SSP for all the full days you are off sick that you normally would have worked.

Your employer will use your average weekly earnings over an 8-week period to work out how much you get. You still qualify if you started your job recently and have not yet received 8 weeks’ pay. Ask your employer to find out more.

### How you’re paid

Your employer pays SSP in the same way they pay your normal wages, such as weekly or monthly.

If you have more than one job, you may get SSP from each employer.

Your employer will take Tax and National Insurance out of your pay.

If you think your SSP payment is wrong, talk to your employer. If you are still not happy, contact the HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) enquiry line.

### The hourly rate for the minimum wage

The amount you are paid depends on your age and if you are an apprentice.

You must be at least:

- school leaving age to get the National Minimum Wage
- aged 21 to get the National Living Wage - the minimum wage will still apply for workers aged 20 and under

## Current rates

The rates change on 1 April every year.

| | 21 and over | 18 to 20 | Under 18 | Apprentice |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| April 2026 | £12.71 | £10.85 | £8 | £8 |
| April 2027 | £13.21 | £11.27 | £8.31 | £8.31 |

### Apprentices

You get the apprentice rate if you are either:

- aged under 19
- aged 19 or over and in your first year of your apprenticeship

You get the minimum wage for your age if you both:

- are aged 19 or over
- have completed the first year of your apprenticeship

## Previous rates

These were the rates for the National Living Wage and the National Minimum Wage starting from April 2019.

### Rates between 1 April 2024 and 31 March 2026

Since 1 April 2024, the National Living Wage applies to people aged 21 and over.

| April 2025 to March 2026 | £12.21 | £10 | £7.55 | £7.55 |
| April 2024 to March 2025 | £11.44 | £8.60 | £6.40 | £6.40 |

Between 1 April 2021 and 31 March 2024, the National Living Wage applied to people aged 23 and over.

| | 23 and over | 21 to 22 | 18 to 20 | Under 18 | Apprentice |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| April 2023 to March 2024 | £10.42 | £10.18 | £7.49 | £5.28 | £5.28 |
| April 2022 to March 2023 | £9.50 | £9.18 | £6.83 | £4.81 | £4.81 |
| April 2021 to March 2022 | £8.91 | £8.36 | £6.56 | £4.62 | £4.30 |

Before 1 April 2021, the National Living Wage applied to people aged 25 and over.

| April 2020 to March 2021 | £8.72 | £8.20 | £6.45 | £4.55 | £4.15 |

### Who gets the minimum wage

Read the information on who has a right to the minimum wage. 

You can use the minimum wage calculator to check if you are being paid the National Minimum Wage or the National Living Wage. 

If you are not getting the National Minimum Wage and you think you should be, contact Acas.

### Winter Fuel Payment

You will get a letter in October or November. This letter will tell you how much Winter Fuel Payment you will get, if you are eligible.

If you do not get a letter but think you are eligible, check if you need to make a claim.

The amount you get depends on when you were born and your circumstances during the ‘qualifying week’. This week is 21 to 27 September 2026.

Any money you get will not affect your other benefits.

### Marriage Allowance

Marriage Allowance lets you move £1,260 of your Personal Allowance to your husband, wife or civil partner. Your Personal Allowance is the amount you can earn before you pay tax.

This lowers their tax by up to £252 in the tax year (6 April to 5 April the next year).

This guide is available in Welsh (Cymraeg).

To benefit as a couple, you must normally have an income below your Personal Allowance. This is usually £12,570. You must be the lower earner to do this.

You can calculate your tax savings as a couple. You should call the Income Tax helpline if you get other income. This includes dividends, savings, or benefits from your job. You can also call if you do not know your taxable income.

If you transfer some of your Personal Allowance, you may have to pay more tax yourself. However, you could still pay less tax as a couple.

### Example

Your income is £11,500 and your Personal Allowance is £12,570. You do not pay tax.

Your partner’s income is £20,000 and their Personal Allowance is £12,570. They pay tax on £7,430. This is their ‘taxable income’. As a couple, you pay Income Tax on £7,430.

When you claim Marriage Allowance, you transfer £1,260 of your Personal Allowance to your partner. Your Personal Allowance becomes £11,310. Your partner gets a reduction of £1,260 on their taxable income.

You will now pay tax on £190. Your partner will pay tax on £6,170. As a couple, you benefit. You pay Income Tax on £6,360 instead of £7,430. This saves you £214 in tax.

## Who can apply

You can get Marriage Allowance if all these things are true:

- you are married or in a civil partnership
- you do not pay Income Tax or your income is less than your Personal Allowance (usually £12,570)
- your partner pays Income Tax at the basic rate, which usually means their income is between £12,571 and £50,270 before they get Marriage Allowance

You cannot claim Marriage Allowance if you live together but you are not married or in a civil partnership.

If you live in Scotland, your partner must pay the starter, basic or intermediate rate. This usually means their income is between £12,571 and £43,662.

It will not change your application for Marriage Allowance if you or your partner:

- are currently getting a pension
- live abroad, as long as you get a Personal Allowance

If you or your partner were born before 6 April 1935, you might benefit more as a couple by applying for Married Couple’s Allowance instead.

You cannot get Marriage Allowance and Married Couple’s Allowance at the same time.

Your partner’s tax bill will be reduced based on the Personal Allowance rate for the years you are backdating.

If your partner has died since 5 April 2022, you can still claim. You must phone the Income Tax helpline. If your partner was the lower earner, the person managing their tax affairs must phone.

### Statutory redundancy pay

You will usually get statutory redundancy pay if you are an employee and you have worked for your employer for 2 years or more.

You will get:

* half a week’s pay for each full year you were under 22
* one week’s pay for each full year you were 22 or older, but under 41
* one and half week’s pay for each full year you were 41 or older

You can count up to 20 years of service.

Your weekly pay is the average you earned each week during the 12 weeks before you got your redundancy notice.

If you were paid less because you were ‘on furlough’ due to coronavirus, your statutory redundancy pay is based on your normal pay.

If you were made redundant on or after 6 April 2026, your weekly pay is capped at £751 and the maximum statutory redundancy pay you can get is £22,530. If you were made redundant before 6 April 2026, these amounts will be lower.

Calculate your redundancy pay.

You have 6 months from the date your job ends to apply for statutory redundancy pay.

## Exceptions

You will not get statutory redundancy pay if:

- your employer offers to keep you in your job
- your employer offers you suitable alternative work and you refuse it without a good reason

You will not get statutory redundancy pay if you are dismissed for misconduct, because this does not count as redundancy.

You will not get statutory redundancy pay if you are in any of these categories:

- former registered dock workers (who are covered by other arrangements) or share fishermen
- crown servants, members of the armed forces or police services
- apprentices who are not employees when their training ends
- a domestic servant who is a member of the employer’s immediate family

## Short-term and temporary lay-offs

You can claim statutory redundancy pay if you are eligible and you have been temporarily laid off, either with no pay or less than half a week’s pay, for either:

- more than 4 weeks in a row 

- more than 6 weeks that do not follow each other in a 13 week period

Write to your employer to tell them you intend to claim statutory redundancy pay. You must do this within 4 weeks of your last non-working day in the 4 or 6 week period.

If your employer does not reject your claim within 7 days of receiving it, write to your employer again to give them your notice.

Your claim may be rejected if your normal work is likely to start within 4 weeks and continue for at least 13 weeks.

## If you pay basic rate Income Tax

If you are a basic rate taxpayer, the rate you pay on gains from 6 April 2026 depends on how much you gained and how much taxable income you have.

You can see the rates and allowance for previous years.

To work out your rate:

- Work out your taxable income. This is your total income minus your Personal Allowance and any Income Tax reliefs you can get.
- Work out your total taxable gains.
- Subtract your tax-free allowance from your total taxable gains.
- Add this remainder to your taxable income.
- If this total amount is within the basic Income Tax band, you will pay 18% on your gains made from 6 April 2026.
- If this total amount is more than the basic Income Tax band, you will pay 24% on the part of your gains above the basic Income Tax band for gains made from 6 April 2026.

### Example 1

You make a gain on or after 6 April 2026. Your taxable income is £20,000 and your taxable gains are £12,600.

First, subtract the Capital Gains tax-free allowance from your taxable gain. For the 2026 to 2027 tax year the allowance is £3,000, which leaves £9,600 to pay tax on.

Add this £9,600 to your taxable income of £20,000. Your combined amount is £29,600. Because £29,600 is less than £37,700 (the basic rate band for the 2026 to 2027 tax year), you pay Capital Gains Tax at 18%.

This means you will pay £1,728 in Capital Gains Tax.

### Example 2

You make a gain on or after 6 April 2026. Your taxable income is £20,000 and your taxable gains are £52,600.

First, subtract the Capital Gains tax-free allowance from your taxable gain. For the 2026 to 2027 tax year the allowance is £3,000, which leaves £49,600 to pay tax on.

Add this £49,600 to your taxable income of £20,000. Your combined amount is £69,600. Because £69,600 is more than £37,700 (the basic rate band for the 2026 to 2027 tax year), you will pay Capital Gains Tax at 18% on £17,700 and then 24% on £31,900.

This means you will pay £10,842.

### Inheritance Tax

Inheritance Tax is a tax on the property, money and possessions of someone who has died. This is called their estate.

You usually do not have to pay Inheritance Tax if either:

*   the value of the estate is less than the £325,000 threshold
*   you leave everything above the £325,000 threshold to your spouse, civil partner, a charity or a community amateur sports club

You may still need to report the value of the estate even if it is less than the threshold.

Your threshold can increase to £500,000 if you give away your home to your children (including adopted, foster or stepchildren) or grandchildren.

If you are married or in a civil partnership and your estate is worth less than your threshold, any unused threshold can be added to your partner’s threshold when you die.

This guide is also available in Welsh (Cymraeg).

## Inheritance Tax rates

The standard Inheritance Tax rate is 40%. You only pay this on the part of your estate that is worth more than the threshold.

### Example

Your estate is worth £500,000 and your tax-free threshold is £325,000. You will pay Inheritance Tax at 40% on £175,000 (£500,000 minus £325,000).

The estate can pay a lower Inheritance Tax rate of 36% on some assets if you leave 10% or more of the ‘net value’ to charity in your will. The net value is the total value of the estate minus any debts.

### Reliefs and exemptions

Some gifts you give while you are alive may be taxed after you die. Depending on when you gave the gift, ‘taper relief’ may mean the Inheritance Tax you pay on the gift is less than 40%.

Other reliefs, such as Business Relief or Agricultural Relief, can let you pass on some assets free of Inheritance Tax or with a smaller bill.

## Who pays the tax to HMRC

Money from your estate is used to pay Inheritance Tax to HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC). The person dealing with your estate pays this. If you have a will, this person is called the 'executor'.

Your beneficiaries (the people who inherit your estate) do not normally pay tax on what they inherit. They may have to pay other related taxes. For example, they may have to pay tax if they get rental income from a house you left them in a will.

People who receive gifts from you might have to pay Inheritance Tax if both of these conditions are met:
* you give away more than £325,000
* you die within 7 years of giving the gift

### Late enrollment penalties

You must sign up for Medicare during your Initial Enrollment Period. You do not have to sign up if you have other coverage that is worth as much as Medicare, such as coverage from an employer. If you do not sign up when you are supposed to, you may have to pay an extra cost. This is called a late enrollment penalty.

Late enrollment penalties:

- Are added to your monthly premium.
- Are not a one-time late fee.
- Are usually charged for as long as you have that type of coverage. For most people, this is a lifetime penalty. The Part A penalty is different.
- Go up the longer you wait to sign up. They are based on how long you go without coverage similar to Medicare. Find out when you should sign up to avoid penalties.

## Part A late enrollment penalty

- Some people must buy Part A because they do not qualify for premium-free Part A. 
- If you must buy Part A, and you do not buy it when you are first eligible for Medicare, your monthly premium may go up 10%.
- You will have to pay the penalty for twice the number of years you did not sign up.

- If you were eligible for Part A for 2 years but did not sign up, you will have to pay the higher premium for 4 years. 
- Usually, you do not have to pay a penalty if you meet certain conditions that allow you to sign up for Part A during a Special Enrollment Period. 
- Find out if you are eligible for a Special Enrollment Period.

## Part B late enrollment penalty

- You will generally not have to pay a Part B penalty if you qualify for a Special Enrollment Period, or if you enroll in a Medicare Savings Program. Learn more about Special Enrollment Periods.
- You will pay an extra 10% for each year you could have signed up for Part B, but did not.
- You may also have to pay a higher premium based on your income.

Example:

If you waited 2 full years (24 months) to sign up for Part B and did not qualify for a Special Enrollment Period, you must pay a 20% late enrollment penalty (10% for each full 12-month period that you could have signed up), plus the standard Part B monthly premium ($202.90 in 2026). 

2026 Calculation:

$202.90 (2026 Part B standard premium) 
+ $40.58 (20% [of $202.90] late enrollment penalty)

$243.48

$243.50 will be your Part B monthly premium for 2026. This amount ($243.48) is rounded up to the nearest $.10 and includes the late enrollment penalty.

## Part D late enrollment penalty

- Generally, you will not have to pay a Part D penalty if:

- You have creditable drug coverage (coverage that is similar in value to Part D) OR
- You qualify for Extra Help

- You will pay an extra 1% for each month (that is 12% a year) if you:

- Do not join a Medicare drug plan when you first get Medicare.
- Go 63 days or more without creditable drug coverage.

- You may also pay a higher premium depending on your income.
- After you join a Medicare drug plan, the plan will tell you if you have to pay a penalty and what your premium will be.
What if I do not agree with the Part D late enrollment penalty?

Example:
If you waited 14 months after you were eligible for Medicare to join a Medicare drug plan, and you did not have creditable drug coverage, you will have to pay a 14% late enrollment penalty in addition to your monthly plan premium. 

- The penalty amount comes from the "national base beneficiary premium" ($38.99 in 2026).
- The national base beneficiary premium changes each year, so your penalty amount may also change each year. This monthly penalty is added for as long as you have Medicare drug coverage, even if you switch plans.

In 2026:

$38.99 (2026 national base beneficiary premium)
X 0.14 (14% penalty)

$5.46 (rounded to the nearest $0.10 = $5.50)
$5.50 will be your monthly penalty for 2026. This amount is added to your plan’s monthly premium for 2026.

## When are Medicare premiums due?

All Medicare bills are due on the 25th of the month. In most cases, you must pay your premium in the same month you get the bill. 

For your payment to be on time, we must get your payment by the due date on your bill. Send your payment at least 5 business days before the due date so we can get it on time.

### What if your Medicare premium payment is late?

If you miss a payment, or if we get your payment late, your next bill will include the amount that is past due.

If you get a Medicare premium bill with “Delinquent Bill” at the top, you must pay the total amount due. If you do not, you will lose your Medicare coverage.

### Choosing a Medicare plan

After you have Medicare Part A (Hospital Insurance) and/or Part B (Medical Insurance), you can pick a Medicare health or drug plan that fits your needs. Use this page to learn if you can join a Medicare health or drug plan, when you can join, and how to join.

## Am I eligible?

To join a Medicare health plan or drug plan, you generally must:

* Have Medicare Part A and/or Part B.
* Be a U.S. citizen or U.S. national, a green card holder, a Cuban-Haitian entrant, or lawfully living in the U.S. as a Compact of Free Association (COFA) migrant.
* Live in the area where the plan is offered.
* Have your Medicare Number and the start dates for your Part A and/or Part B coverage. You can find this information on your Medicare card.

## When can I join?

You can only join, switch, or drop a Medicare Advantage Plan (Part C) with or without drug coverage, other Medicare health plan, or Medicare drug plan at certain times. These times are called enrollment periods.

## Initial Enrollment Period

This period usually happens when you turn 65.

It lasts for 7 months. It starts 3 months before you turn 65. It ends 3 months after the month you turn 65. You may be able to get Medicare earlier if you have a disability, End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD), or ALS (also called Lou Gehrig’s disease). You can learn more about when you can sign up in these situations.

You can join any plan, but you need:

- Both Part A and Part B to join a Medicare Advantage Plan with or without drug coverage.
- Either Part A or Part B to join a Medicare drug plan.

When your coverage starts:

- If you request to join a plan before your Part A and/or Part B starts: Your plan coverage starts the same day as when your Part A and/or Part B starts.
- If you request to join a plan after your Part A and/or Part B starts: Your plan coverage starts the first of the month after the plan gets your request.

## Initial Enrollment Period – New to Part B

If you have Part A and are adding Part B later:

This period starts 3 months before the month you are first eligible for both Part A and Part B. You will have 2 months after you get both Part A and Part B for the first time to join a plan.

You can:

* Join any Medicare Advantage Plan with or without drug coverage.

Coverage starts:

* Generally, the first of the month after the plan gets your request to join.

If you joined a Medicare Advantage Plan during your Initial Enrollment Period, you can change to another Medicare Advantage Plan (with or without drug coverage) or go back to Original Medicare (with or without a drug plan) within the first 3 months you have Medicare Part A and Part B.

### If you are still working at age 65

If you or your spouse are still working when you turn 65, Medicare works a little differently. Do you need a refresher on Medicare basics?

## Do I need to sign up for Medicare when I turn 65?

You can answer a few questions to see when you should sign up or look at the situations below.

Find out when to sign up

If you do not have to pay a premium for Part A (Hospital Insurance), you can choose to sign up when you turn 65 or anytime later. Will I have to pay a premium for Part A?

### If you (or your spouse) have health insurance from a job:

If you or your spouse are still working, you may be able to wait to sign up for Medicare without paying a late enrollment penalty. This applies if you have group health insurance that is available to everyone at the company.

- If you do not have to pay a premium for Part A (Hospital Insurance), you can choose to sign up when you turn 65 or anytime later. Do I qualify?
- You can wait until you (or your spouse) stop working or lose your health insurance, if that happens first, to sign up for Part B (Medical Insurance). You will not pay a late enrollment penalty this way.
- Once you stop working or lose your health insurance, if that happens first, you have an 8-month Special Enrollment Period (SEP) to sign up for Medicare or add Part B to existing Part A coverage. The SEP starts when you stop working or lose insurance, even if you choose COBRA or other coverage that is not Medicare.

Ask the employer who provides your health insurance if you need to sign up for Part A (Hospital Insurance) and Part B (Medical Insurance) when you turn 65. If you do not sign up for Part A and Part B, your job-based insurance might not cover your costs for services you get. This applies if you are self-employed or have health insurance that is not available to everyone at the company, like retiree coverage.

Ask your insurance provider if your coverage is employer group health plan coverage as defined by the IRS. If it is not, sign up for Medicare when you turn 65 to avoid a monthly Part B late enrollment penalty.

If you have retiree coverage from a previous job, it may not pay for your health services if you do not have both Medicare Part A (Hospital Insurance) and Part B (Medical Insurance). Ask your benefits administrator how your retiree coverage works with Medicare.

Do not risk losing your retiree coverage. Check before joining a plan.
The employer may offer coverage when you have Medicare, like a supplemental plan, drug coverage, or a Medicare Advantage Plan. If they do, ask if you or your family will lose your retiree coverage if you join a plan the employer does not offer. Get more information about retiree coverage & Medicare.

### If you have health insurance that is not from a job: Like insurance from Medicaid, Marketplace, or another private company.

Answer a few questions to find out when to sign up for Medicare and get other important information, based on the specific type of coverage you have.

The rules change based on what type of other health insurance you have. Contact your health insurance plan to get more information. This includes insurance you bought with a stipend from work.

Ask your health insurance company if you need to sign up for Part A (Hospital Insurance) and Part B (Medical Insurance) when you turn 65. Some private insurance companies have rules that lower what they pay, or do not pay at all, for services you get if you are eligible for other coverage, like Medicare. Once you sign up, Medicare pays first.

### If you have COBRA coverage:

If your job offered you COBRA coverage after your employment ended, or after you lost coverage as the dependent of the covered employee, and you have not signed up for Medicare yet, the rules may change.

- Sign up for Medicare when you turn 65 to avoid gaps in coverage and a monthly Part B late enrollment penalty.
- Your COBRA coverage will probably end once you sign up.

Do not wait until your COBRA coverage ends to sign up for Part B. COBRA coverage does not extend your limited time to sign up for Medicare.

Get important information about COBRA and Medicare. This also applies if you got COBRA after you signed up for Medicare.

COBRA pays after Medicare, unless you have End-Stage Renal Disease.

Get important information about COBRA and Medicare.

### If you don’t have health insurance: And you’re still working.

- Sign up for both Part A (Hospital Insurance) and Part B (Medical Insurance) when you are first eligible, which is usually when you turn 65. If you sign up later, you may have to pay a penalty.
- If you cannot afford insurance, there are ways to get help paying costs.

## How do I sign up for Medicare when I'm ready?

How you sign up depends on if you already have Part A (Hospital Insurance) coverage or if you are signing up for both Part A and Part B (Medical Insurance). You can get forms and see ways to sign up.

Your coverage will start the month after Social Security (or the Railroad Retirement Board) processes your completed form.

Before you sign up:

### When your Medicare coverage starts

Your Medicare coverage start date depends on two things:

*   When you sign up. 
*   Which enrollment period you use.

## Your first chance to sign up (Initial Enrollment Period)

You can usually sign up when you turn 65. We call this your Initial Enrollment Period. It lasts for 7 months. It starts 3 months before the month you turn 65. It ends 3 months after the month you turn 65. 

If your birthday is on the first of the month, the rules change. 

### Avoid the penalty
If you miss your 7-month Initial Enrollment Period, you may have to wait to sign up. You may also have to pay a monthly late enrollment penalty. You must pay this for as long as you have Part B coverage. The penalty goes up the longer you wait. You may also have to pay a penalty if you have to pay for Part A, which is called “Premium-Part A.” Learn more about how to avoid late enrollment penalties. 

### When your coverage starts

The date your coverage starts depends on which month you sign up. Coverage always starts on the first of the month.

If you qualify for premium-free Part A: Your Part A coverage starts the month you turn 65. If your birthday is on the first of the month, coverage starts the month before you turn 65.

Part B (and Premium-Part A): Coverage starts based on the month you sign up:

| If you sign up: | Coverage starts: |

| Before the month you turn 65 | The month you turn 65 |
| The month you turn 65, or during the 3 months after | The next month |

### Signing up for premium-free Part A later

You can sign up for Part A any time after you turn 65. Your Part A coverage starts 6 months back from when you sign up or when you apply for benefits from Social Security or the Railroad Retirement Board. Coverage cannot start earlier than the month you turned 65.

If you have a Health Savings Account (HSA), check your rules. 

After your Initial Enrollment Period ends, you can only sign up for Part B and Premium-Part A during one of the other enrollment periods.

## Between January 1-March 31 each year (General Enrollment Period)

You can sign up between January 1-March 31 each year. We call this the General Enrollment Period. Your coverage will start the month after you sign up. You may have to pay a monthly late enrollment penalty if you do not qualify for a Special Enrollment Period.

### Your costs for Medicare drug coverage

Your total costs depend on the plan you choose. Depending on the plan, you could pay:

*   Premium: A monthly amount you pay for coverage. You pay this whether you get drugs or not.
    *   Your premium depends on the plan you choose.
    *   You may have to pay more if your income is high.
    *   If you have to pay a Part D late enrollment penalty, it will be added to your monthly premium.
*   Deductible: An amount you pay for covered drugs and items each year before your plan starts to pay. 
    *   Your deductible depends on the plan you choose. 
    *   No Medicare drug plan may have a deductible more than $700 in 2027 ($615 in 2026).
    *   Some plans have no deductible.
*   Copayment: A fixed amount you pay for a drug at the pharmacy.
*   Coinsurance: A percentage you pay for a drug at the pharmacy.

Even if you do not take many drugs now, or your drug costs are low, consider a drug plan with a low monthly premium to avoid the late enrollment penalty. All plans must cover a wide range of drugs that people with Medicare take.

## Medicare drug coverage stages

Medicare drug plans and Medicare Advantage Plans with drug coverage generally have 3 stages:

* Deductible stage: If your plan has a deductible, you pay all costs for your drugs until you reach the full deductible amount. No plan may have a deductible more than $615 in 2026 ($700 in 2027). Some plans do not have a deductible.
* Initial coverage stage: After you reach your full deductible (if your plan has one), you will pay 25% of the cost for your generic and brand-name drugs. You stay in this stage until your out-of-pocket spending on covered Part D drugs reaches $2,100 in 2026 ($2,400 in 2027). This includes certain payments made on your behalf, like through the Extra Help program. After you reach that amount, you will automatically get catastrophic coverage.
* Catastrophic coverage stage: You will not have to pay out-of-pocket for covered Part D drugs for the rest of the calendar year.

When you have Medicare drug coverage, you will get an Explanation of Benefits (EOB). You will get it the month after the pharmacy bills your plan. Your EOB shows the prescriptions you filled. It shows what your plan paid. It shows what you and others have paid. It shows your coverage stage. It also shows what counts toward your out-of-pocket costs and your total drug costs.

## How do I pay my plan’s premium?

You can choose to pay your premium using these ways:

*   Have your plan take the money from your checking or savings account.
*   Charge it to a credit or debit card. Fees may apply.
*   Have your plan send you a bill each month. Some plans bill in advance for coverage for the next month. Send your payment to the plan. Do not send it to Medicare. Contact your plan to get their payment address.
*   Have your premium taken out of your Social Security payment. Contact your plan to ask for this. Do not contact Social Security. It may take up to 3 months to start. If your premiums were not taken out of your Social Security payment until 1 or 2 months after you joined a Medicare drug plan, you will get a bill for the months the premiums were not taken out. You must pay your drug plan’s monthly premium directly to your plan for those months. Your plan will tell you when they set up the withholding from your Social Security payment.

## How can I lower my drug costs?

If you qualify, there are programs that can lower your drug costs:

- Medicaid: This is a federal and state program. It helps pay medical costs for some people with limited income and resources. Each state has its own income and resource rules to decide who is eligible. Contact your state to find out if you are eligible.
- Extra Help: This is a Medicare program that helps pay your drug costs. You automatically qualify for Extra Help if you qualify for Medicaid, one of the Medicare Savings Programs, or Supplemental Security Income (SSI) benefits from Social Security. If you do not automatically qualify for Extra Help, you can apply.
- Medicare’s Limited Income Newly Eligible Transition (LI NET): This is a Medicare program. It gives temporary Medicare Part D drug coverage to people who qualify for Extra Help or Medicaid but who are not enrolled in a Medicare drug plan yet. LI NET covers all Part D covered drugs, and there are no network pharmacy restrictions.
- State Pharmaceutical Assistance Programs (SPAP): These programs provide coverage from your state (or the U.S. Virgin Islands). They help pay your drug plan premiums and/or cost sharing. SPAP contributions may count toward your Medicare drug coverage out-of-pocket limit. Eligibility depends on the specific rules of each program.
- Pharmaceutical Assistance Programs (sometimes called Patient Assistance Programs (PAPs)): Some drug companies offer programs to help pay for medications for people enrolled in Medicare drug coverage (Part D). Find out if there is a Pharmaceutical Assistance Program (PAP) that can lower prescription costs for the drugs you take. Each company has different rules to join their program. Contact the company to find out if you are eligible and start getting help.

The Medicare Prescription Payment Plan is a new payment option. It works with your current Medicare drug coverage. It helps you manage your out-of-pocket costs for drugs covered by your plan. It does this by spreading the costs across the calendar year (January–December). This payment option might help you manage your monthly expenses, but it does not save you money or lower your drug costs.

## What’s the Part D late enrollment penalty?

The Part D late enrollment penalty is a charge that is permanently added to your Medicare drug coverage (Part D) premium. You may owe this penalty if there is a period of 63 or more days in a row when you do not have Medicare drug coverage or other creditable prescription drug coverage after your Initial Enrollment Period ends. 

After you join a Medicare drug plan, the plan will tell you if you must pay a penalty and what your premium will be. You will generally have to pay the penalty for as long as you have Medicare drug coverage.

### How much is the Part D late enrollment penalty?

To calculate the penalty, multiply 1% of the “national base beneficiary premium” ($38.99 in 2026) by the number of full, uncovered months you were eligible to join Medicare drug coverage but did not (and did not have other creditable prescription drug coverage). 

That amount is rounded to the nearest $.10 and added to your monthly premium. Because the “national base beneficiary premium” may go up each year, your penalty amount may also go up each year.

Example: If you waited 14 months after you were eligible for Medicare to join a Medicare drug plan, and you did not have creditable drug coverage, you must pay a 14% late enrollment penalty on top of your monthly plan premium.

The Part D late enrollment penalty is added to your premium for as long as you have Medicare drug coverage, even if you switch plans. However, you do not pay a late enrollment penalty if you get Extra Help.

## Appeal when a hospital changes your status from "inpatient" to "outpatient with observation services"

A court order gives you the right to appeal if a hospital changes your status from "inpatient" to "outpatient" and you meet certain rules.

You can ask for an appeal if:
* You were admitted to the hospital as an inpatient on or after January 1, 2009.
* Your status was changed to "outpatient getting observation services."
* You meet certain other rules. 

Learn how to file this type of appeal.

You can ask for a fast appeal while you are still in the hospital if:
* You were admitted to the hospital as an inpatient.
* The hospital changed your status to "outpatient getting observation services." 

Learn how to file this type of appeal.

### Why does hospital status matter?

Your hospital status affects how much you pay for hospital services. Your hospital status may also affect whether Medicare will cover care you get in a skilled nursing facility (SNF) after your hospital stay.
